title: Nudging healthy food choices: a field experiment at the train station
abstract: BACKGROUND: Recognizing the mindless nature of many food decisions, it has been suggested that attempts to increase healthy eating should not focus on convincing people what is 'right' but rather aim to adjust the environment such that people are automatically directed toward healthy choices. This study investigated a nudge aiming to promote healthy food choices in train station snack shops. METHODS: The nudge involved a repositioning of food products: healthy foods were placed at the cash register desk, while keeping unhealthy products available elsewhere in the shop. Three snack shops were included: a control condition; a nudge condition repositioning healthy products and a nudge + disclosure condition employing the same nudge together with an explanatory sign. Next to examining its effectiveness during 1 week, the study assessed customers' acceptance of the nudge. RESULTS: Controlling for a baseline week, more healthy (but not fewer unhealthy) products were sold in both nudge conditions, with no difference between the nudge and the nudge + disclosure condition. A majority of customers reported positive attitudes toward the nudge. CONCLUSIONS: Repositioning healthy foods is a simple, effective and well-accepted nudge to increase healthy purchases. Moreover, disclosing its purpose does not impact on effectiveness.

claims.text: Repositioning healthy foods at the cash register desk resulted in more healthy products being sold compared to baseline in train station snack shops.
Repositioning healthy foods at the cash register desk did not result in fewer unhealthy products being sold compared to baseline.
There was no difference in the sales of healthy products between the nudge condition and the nudge plus disclosure condition.
A majority of customers reported positive attitudes toward the repositioning nudge.

methodologies.name: Field experiment with product repositioning and disclosure
methodologies.description: A field experiment conducted across three train station snack shops comparing sales during an intervention week against a baseline week across three conditions: control, nudge (healthy foods placed at the cash register desk), and nudge + disclosure (same repositioning plus an explanatory sign).
datasets: Train station snack shop sales and customer survey data
conditions: Nudge condition (healthy foods placed at the cash register desk)
Nudge + disclosure condition (repositioning with an explanatory sign)
